cards.explanation: The answer is a prisoner of Christ Jesus. Paul, who is writing this letter, opens with "…a prisoner of Christ Jesus…" Before he asks for anything, he tells Philemon right where he's sitting. I think that sets a humble tone for everything that follows. Nobody gets a more honest introduction than that.
The answer is in a house. Verse 2 says "…the church that meets at your house…" That means Philemon's house, friends. Believers gathered at home. I hope Philemon owned enough chairs.
The answer is False, friends. Paul writes, "I always thank my God, remembering you in my prayers…" Not once in a while, ALWAYS. Imagine being the person somebody never stops thanking God for.

The answer is his faith in Jesus and his love for the saints. Paul says he hears about "…your faith in the Lord Jesus and your love for all the saints." That's the news that reaches him. Faith toward Jesus and love toward God's people, side by side. Good news travels, friends, even to a man in chains.

The answer is True. Paul says to Philemon, "…you, brother, have refreshed the hearts of the saints." The saints are God's people, and Philemon's love has lifted them. Paul calls him brother right there, too. I bet that sentence made Philemon smile.

The answer is appeal. Paul writes, "I prefer to appeal on the basis of love." He's just said he's bold enough to order Philemon, and then he sets that aside. He picks the gentler road on purpose. A man with a strong hand choosing a soft ask, friends, that's something.

The answer is while he was in chains. Paul says Onesimus is his child, "…whose father I became while I was in chains." Onesimus is the man Paul is appealing for in this letter. So Paul's chains didn't stop something good from happening. Paul calls him his child, and that's a lot of love packed into one word.

The answer is that he was useless and now he's useful. Paul writes, "Formerly he was useless to you, but now he has become useful both to you and to me." He says it to Philemon and about himself too. Both of them benefit now. That's quite the turnaround for one man.

The answer is False. Paul writes, "I would have liked to keep him with me, so that on your behalf he could minister to me in my chains for the gospel." He wanted Onesimus close, friends. And he sends him back anyway.

The answer is so Philemon's goodness comes by free will. Paul says he didn't want to act without consent "…so that your goodness will not be out of compulsion, but by your own free will." He wants Philemon's good deed to be Philemon's own. I think that's why he asks instead of orders. A gift tastes better when nobody twisted your arm, friends.

The answer is good. Paul says Onesimus was separated "…so that you might have him back for good…" For good means for keeps, friends. Paul only says perhaps, so he's offering a way to see it, not announcing a fact.

The answer is brother. Paul says "…no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a beloved brother." That's a big change in how Philemon might see Onesimus. And Paul adds that he's beloved to Philemon both in person and in the Lord. A brother is family, friends.

The answer is True. Paul writes, "So if you consider me a partner, receive him as you would receive me." That's a big ask, and he's tying it to their friendship. Whatever welcome Philemon would give Paul, Paul asks him to give Onesimus. He's not mentioning that lightly, friends.

The answer is account. Paul says, "But if he has wronged you in any way or owes you anything, charge it to my account." He's offering to cover it if there's anything owed. I think that's a lot of love for one letter. A man in chains offering to pay the tab if there is one.

The answer is True. Paul writes, "Yes, brother, let me have some benefit from you in the Lord. Refresh my heart in Christ." Earlier he told Philemon he had refreshed the hearts of the saints. Now he asks for the same refreshing for himself. Even a man in chains likes a little encouragement, friends.

The answer is that Philemon will do even more than Paul asks. Paul writes, "Confident of your obedience, I write to you, knowing that you will do even more than I ask." He's not just hoping for the minimum. He expects Philemon to go beyond what he asked. That's a big vote of confidence, friends.

The answer is his fellow prisoner in Christ Jesus. Paul writes, "Epaphras, my fellow prisoner in Christ Jesus, sends you greetings…" That's the title the text gives him. Paul passes his greetings along so Philemon hears from him. I think a hello from a fellow prisoner means a lot.
